title: Hakone Is Five Different Places — Choose Your Ryokan by What You Actually Want to Do
description: Most visitors rush the Hakone loop in a day from Tokyo and see a fraction of it. Hakone is not one destination but five areas strung along a slow transport circuit, and where you sleep decides what you get to do. Here is each area, the ryokan worth booking in it, and how a ryokan night actually works.
intro: Hakone is the most popular overnight trip from Tokyo, and the way most people do it is a mistake: out on the morning train, round the loop — mountain railway, cable car, ropeway over the volcano, pirate ship across the lake — and back to Shinjuku by evening, having spent most of the day in transit. The loop is genuinely good, but it is designed to be taken slowly, and the reason to stay the night is not just the ryokan. It is that Hakone is not a single place. It is five distinct areas — the hot spring town at the entrance, the museum-and-grassland plateau, the volcanic valley, the lake with the Mount Fuji view, and the quiet middle — connected by a transport network that is itself part of the attraction. Where you sleep determines which of them you actually experience, because the last leg of the loop takes a while and you will not want to do it twice. This guide takes each area in turn, with the ryokan or hotel worth booking there, and covers the parts of a ryokan stay that surprise first-time visitors — starting with the fact that dinner is at six.
listHeading: Hakone by area, and where to stay in each

buyingGuide.title: Understand the loop before you pick an area
buyingGuide.body: Hakone's attractions are strung along a one-way circuit that most people travel in the same direction: from Hakone-Yumoto, a switchback mountain railway climbs to Gora, a funicular continues to Sounzan, a ropeway crosses above the volcanic valley at Owakudani, and a sightseeing boat crosses Lake Ashi to Moto-Hakone, from where buses return to Yumoto. Completing it takes the better part of a day at a comfortable pace. This matters for booking, because a ryokan at the far end of the loop means an hour or more of travel with your luggage at each end. Decide which parts you care about, then choose accommodation on that section rather than by price alone.

buyingGuide.title: Get the Hakone Free Pass, and consider the Romancecar
buyingGuide.body: The Hakone Free Pass covers unlimited use of the mountain railway, cable car, ropeway, sightseeing boats and local buses, plus the return journey from Shinjuku, in two-day and three-day versions. If you intend to do any part of the loop it pays for itself quickly, and it removes the friction of buying tickets at each transfer. The Odakyu Romancecar runs from Shinjuku to Hakone-Yumoto in around 85 minutes with reserved seats and luggage space; the pass covers the base fare but the reserved-seat supplement is extra and worth paying with suitcases. Buy the pass before you travel or at Shinjuku Station rather than in Hakone.

buyingGuide.title: Do not drag suitcases around the loop
buyingGuide.body: This is the practical mistake that ruins the day. The mountain railway, ropeway and boats are not built for large luggage, and the transfers involve stairs. Use a luggage delivery service — there is one operating from Hakone-Yumoto Station that will deliver bags to hotels in the area, usually with a morning cut-off for same-day arrival — or leave your main case at your Tokyo hotel and travel to Hakone with an overnight bag. Coin lockers exist at Hakone-Yumoto but fill early. Sorting this out in advance is the difference between the loop being a pleasure and a chore.

buyingGuide.title: How a ryokan night actually works
buyingGuide.body: A traditional inn runs on a schedule, and it is not the one you are used to. Check-in is usually from around 15:00 and you are expected to arrive before dinner, which is typically served between 17:30 and 19:00 — early by most visitors' standards, and not something you can push back on the night. The meal is kaiseki, a long sequence of small seasonal courses, and it is a substantial part of what you are paying for. You will be given a yukata to wear around the building, including to dinner. At many inns staff lay out futon bedding in your room while you eat, so the room you return to looks different from the one you left. Plan your day so you are back by mid-afternoon rather than treating the inn as somewhere to sleep.

buyingGuide.title: Ryokan price per person, and the rate includes two meals
buyingGuide.body: Traditional inns quote per person, not per room, and the rate normally includes both dinner and breakfast. This makes the headline figure look alarming next to a city hotel until you account for a multi-course dinner and breakfast for everyone. It also means the price does not halve if two of you share a room. When comparing options here, work out the total for your party including meals rather than reading the advertised number. If you would rather eat in town, some properties offer room-only rates, but in Hakone the dinner is usually the point rather than an add-on.

buyingGuide.title: Communal baths, private baths, and the swimsuit option
buyingGuide.body: The hot springs are the reason to come, and they take three forms here. Public baths are segregated by gender and bathed in naked, with a thorough wash at the shower stations first; some properties restrict guests with visible tattoos, so check if that applies to you. A room with its own open-air bath removes both the tattoo question and any hesitation about communal bathing, which is why they are worth the premium for many overseas couples. And Yunessun, in the Kowakidani area, is a hot spring park where you wear a swimsuit — an entirely different proposition, and the easiest introduction if the naked communal bath is a step too far.

buyingGuide.title: Be realistic about Mount Fuji
buyingGuide.body: Many people book Hakone expecting the view of Fuji across Lake Ashi, and it is genuinely spectacular when it appears. It also frequently does not. The mountain is commonly obscured by cloud, particularly in summer, and visibility is best in the clear, dry air from late autumn through winter and in the early morning. Treat a Fuji view as a bonus rather than the reason for the trip, and if it matters to you, book a lakeside property, stay two nights to have two mornings, and look early. The rest of Hakone is worth the journey regardless of what the weather does.

places.name: Hakone Yumoto Onsen Tenseien
places.japaneseName: 箱根湯本温泉 天成園
places.area: Hakone-Yumoto · the entrance to Hakone, walkable from the station
places.description: The most practical base, and the one to book if you are arriving from Tokyo with luggage. Hakone-Yumoto is where the Romancecar arrives and where the loop begins, so staying here means you are not carrying bags up the mountain and back. Tenseien is a large, long-established property with an unusually good bathing complex — a rooftop open-air bath with a view over the valley, and a garden with a waterfall — which is a lot of hot spring for the price. It is popular as a day-use bathhouse too, so as a staying guest you get the run of facilities most inns cannot match. Around 4,000 domestic reviews. Best if you want one uncomplicated night and a full day on the loop, rather than a remote retreat.
pros: At the entrance to Hakone — no luggage-hauling up the mountain
Large bathing complex including a rooftop open-air bath
Easiest base for doing the full loop in a day
cons: About 15 minutes on foot from the station; the shuttle is chargeable
A large, busy property — the baths get crowded in peak season

places.name: Odakyu Hotel de Yama
places.japaneseName: 小田急 山のホテル
places.area: Lake Ashi, Moto-Hakone · gardens with the Mount Fuji view
places.description: The choice if the lake and the Fuji view are what brought you here. It sits on the shore of Lake Ashi at Moto-Hakone, the far end of the loop, in gardens that are themselves a destination — the azaleas in spring are among the best in the region. This is the postcard side of Hakone: the sightseeing boats, the lakeside walk to the torii gate standing in the water, and the Narukawa Art Museum next door. Being an Odakyu property, it fits neatly with the Free Pass and Romancecar. It rates around 4.5 out of 5. The trade-off is distance: Moto-Hakone is roughly an hour from Yumoto, so either arrive with light luggage or use a delivery service.
pros: On Lake Ashi with garden views towards Mount Fuji on clear days
Walking distance to the lakeside torii gate and the boat pier
cons: Roughly an hour from Hakone-Yumoto — awkward with suitcases
Premium pricing, and the Fuji view depends entirely on weather

places.name: Hakone Kowakien Tenyu
places.area: Ninotaira, Kowakidani · a private open-air bath in every room
places.description: The one to book if the idea of a communal naked bath is what is holding you back — or if you simply want the hot spring to yourself. Every room has its own open-air hot spring bath, so you can bathe privately, at any hour, with a view over the gorge, and the tattoo question does not arise. There is also a dramatic infinity-style public bath if you do want the full experience. At around 4.7 out of 5 it is the highest rated property in this guide, and the standard of food and service matches. It sits mid-loop near Gora, so the museums and the ropeway are close. This is the expensive option here by a wide margin, and it is the one people book for an anniversary.
pros: Private open-air hot spring bath in every room
Mid-loop position, close to Gora and the museums
cons: By far the most expensive option in this guide
Rooms with the best views book out months ahead

places.name: Hakone Hotel Kowakien
places.area: Ninotaira, Kowakidani · unlimited access to the Yunessun spa park
places.description: The pick for a day that is more water park than contemplative soak. Guests get unlimited entry to Yunessun next door — a hot spring complex where you wear a swimsuit, with outdoor pools, slides and a run of novelty baths — and to Mori no Yu, the traditional naked bathing side. That combination is genuinely useful for overseas visitors: you can spend the afternoon somewhere no etiquette anxiety applies, then try the conventional hot spring in the evening. There is a large buffet rather than a formal kaiseki, which suits anyone who would rather not sit through a nine-course dinner. Rated around 4.4 out of 5. It is lively rather than serene — choose it on that basis.
pros: Unlimited Yunessun access — a swimsuit hot spring park, no etiquette needed
Also covers the traditional naked baths at Mori no Yu
Buffet dining rather than a fixed multi-course dinner
cons: Yunessun is busy at weekends and in Japanese holiday periods
Lively and family-heavy — not the quiet ryokan experience

places.name: nol hakone myojindai
places.area: Miyagino · between Gora and Sengokuhara, design-led
places.description: The modern alternative, for anyone who wants Hakone without the full traditional ceremony. Recently rebranded as a design hotel, it trades the formal ryokan template for a contemporary one — the aesthetic is restrained and current, and breakfast is a highlight rather than an afterthought. Its position in Miyagino, between Gora and Sengokuhara, is quietly one of the best on this list for getting around: the museums, the ropeway and the grasslands are all within reach without committing to either end of the loop. It rates around 4.6 out of 5, though on a smaller number of reviews than the established properties here. Choose it if a nine-course kaiseki in a yukata is not what you came for.
pros: Contemporary design rather than the traditional ryokan format
Well placed between Gora and Sengokuhara for reaching both
Rated around 4.6/5, with breakfast singled out
cons: Recently rebranded, so fewer reviews to judge it on
Not the large communal bathing complex some visitors want

places.name: Hakone Retreat fore
places.area: Sengokuhara · the museum and grassland plateau
places.description: The base for the side of Hakone that is about art and open country rather than hot spring towns. Sengokuhara is a high plateau holding the Pola Museum of Art, the Hakone Glass Forest, the wetlands botanical garden, and the silver grass fields that turn gold in autumn — a genuinely different landscape from the wooded gorges below, and the part of Hakone most day-trippers never reach. The property sits in forest and is designed to feel like a retreat rather than an inn, which suits two people who want to walk during the day and be somewhere quiet at night. Rated around 4.4 out of 5. Sengokuhara is bus-dependent, so factor that into your plan.
pros: Best base for the Pola Museum, Glass Forest and the grasslands
A forest setting designed as a retreat rather than a hotel
Reaches the part of Hakone most day visitors skip
cons: Sengokuhara is away from the railway — you rely on buses
No large communal bathing complex in the traditional style

faq.question: Can I do Hakone as a day trip from Tokyo?
faq.answer: You can, and most people do, but you will spend the majority of the day travelling. The loop — mountain railway, cable car, ropeway, boat, bus — takes the better part of a day at a comfortable pace, which leaves little time for the museums, the lake or a proper hot spring. Staying one night turns it into a trip rather than an endurance exercise, and two nights lets you take the loop in one direction and explore an area properly. Since a ryokan rate includes dinner and breakfast, the overnight cost is less of a jump than it first appears.

faq.question: Is the Hakone Free Pass worth buying?
faq.answer: If you plan to use any significant part of the loop, yes. It covers unlimited travel on the mountain railway, cable car, ropeway, sightseeing boats and local buses, plus the return trip from Shinjuku, and comes in two-day and three-day versions. Buying each leg individually costs more and means queueing at every transfer. Buy it before you travel or at Shinjuku Station. Note that the Romancecar's reserved-seat supplement is separate from the pass — worth paying if you are carrying luggage, since it guarantees a seat and space for bags.

faq.question: What actually happens at a ryokan in the evening?
faq.answer: Check in from around 15:00, change into the yukata provided, and use the baths before dinner. Dinner is usually served between 17:30 and 19:00 — earlier than most visitors expect, and generally not flexible — and takes the form of kaiseki, a long sequence of small seasonal dishes. You wear the yukata to dinner; this is normal, not a costume. At many inns, staff lay out futon bedding in your room while you are eating, so you return to a different arrangement. Breakfast is also early. The main adjustment is planning your day around being back by mid-afternoon.

faq.question: I have tattoos. Can I use the hot springs?
faq.answer: It depends on the property, so check before booking rather than at the changing room. Some Hakone inns restrict guests with visible tattoos in their public baths, others do not, and the policy is not always stated in English. The reliable solution is a room with its own private open-air bath — Hakone Kowakien Tenyu in this guide has one in every room — which removes the question entirely. Yunessun is another option, since it is a swimsuit facility rather than a traditional bathhouse. If you have small tattoos, some places accept waterproof covering patches, but this is not universal.

faq.question: Will I see Mount Fuji?
faq.answer: Possibly, but do not count on it. The classic view is across Lake Ashi from the Moto-Hakone side, and when the mountain is out it is genuinely one of Japan's great sights. It is also hidden by cloud a great deal of the time, especially in summer. The clearest conditions come in the dry air of late autumn and winter, and early morning is generally better than afternoon. If it matters to you, stay lakeside, allow two mornings, and look early. Everything else in Hakone — the volcanic valley, the museums, the hot springs — is unaffected by the weather.

faq.question: What is Yunessun, and is it a real onsen?
faq.answer: Yunessun is a hot spring park in the Kowakidani area where you wear a swimsuit, with outdoor pools, water slides and a series of novelty baths that have included wine, coffee and green tea. The water is genuine hot spring water, but the experience is closer to a water park than to a traditional bathhouse. For overseas visitors it has a specific use: it lets you enjoy Hakone's hot springs with no bathing etiquette to navigate and no issue with tattoos. The same complex includes Mori no Yu, a conventional naked bathing area, if you want to try both in one day.
